description: A thicket-forming raspberry of the wet lowland, 1.5-3.5 m, its upright golden-brown canes spreading by rhizomes into dense stands along the streams and under the alders. Its magenta flowers open in March before most plants stir and its soft fruits, salmon-orange to deep red, are the first berries of the year.

season_notes.winter: Bare, golden-brown, shreddy canes with a few weak prickles.
season_notes.spring: Magenta flowers from March, visited by the first rufous hummingbirds; leaves of three toothed leaflets unfold.
season_notes.summer: Raspberry-like fruits ripen yellow-orange to red in June and July.
season_notes.fall: Leaves yellow and fall in October.

riparian.water: Wants moist to wet ground: streambanks, river terraces, seeps and forest openings, and with red alder wherever it grows (FEIS).

targets.from: judgement values from the drafter's reading of the sources and knowledge of the species (2026-11-04), no photographs measured; to be replaced by photo measurements: a dense, head-high thicket of erect, arching canes, leafy from the top third down; much more upright than the trailing blackberry template

notes: Grown from the California blackberry (same genus, trifoliate leaves, cane architecture) as a taller, erect, less sprawling plant: crown width 1.0 of height against the template's 2.0, canes spreading 30 degrees. Leaves of three sharply toothed leaflets, 10-20 cm across the whole leaf; flowers magenta, single or in twos to fours, March to June; fruit 1.5-2 cm, yellowish to orange to deep red, June-July in the south of the range, July-August in the north and high (FEIS). Its rhizome spread into whole stands is not grown (one plant per placement). FEIS: black bears eat and spread the fruit, elk and deer browse the young leaves and stems, and birds, Pacific martens, banana slugs, rodents and rufous hummingbirds (pollinators) use it; Swainson's thrush is called the salmonberry bird in the region. Only the bear, coyote, deer and Steller's jay are in the animal library.
